q: Read verses 1–7 (The first vial is poured out on the earth, the second on the sea, the third on the rivers and fountains). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–11 (The fourth on the sun, the fifth on the seat of the beast), what do you learn about sacrifice and atonement?
Verse 15 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 Thessalonians 5:2–3. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Armageddon’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: One of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed.
And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.
ch.s: This chapter covers: One of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed (vv. 1–6); And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns (vv. 7–18).
ch.mh: Rome clearly appears to be meant in this chapter.
q: Read verses 1–6 (One of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 7–18 (And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns), what do you learn about leadership and kingship?
Verse 14 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Romans 8:30. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of god's sovereignty in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us avoid the mysteries of iniquity, and study diligently the great mystery of godliness, that we may learn humility and gratitude from the example of Christ.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.

o: Another angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon.
A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues.
The lamentations over her.
The church called upon to rejoice in her utter ruin.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.

In Rev. 14:8; 16:19; 17:5; and 18:2, "Babylon" is supposed to mean Rome, not considered as pagan, but as the prolongation of the ancient power in the papal form. Rome, pagan and papal, is regarded as one power.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Another angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon (vv. 1–3); A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues (vv. 4–8); The lamentations over her (vv. 9–19); The church called upon to rejoice in her utter ruin (vv. 20–24). Places: Babylon.
ch.mh: The downfal and destruction of the mystical Babylon are determined in the counsels of God.
q: Read verses 1–3 (Another angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 4–8 (A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues), what do you learn about grace and mercy?
Verse 20 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Revelation 6:10. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us take warning from the things which brought others to destruction, and let us set our affections on things above, when we consider the changeable nature of earthly things.
ch.a: Show the same mercy you have received to someone who does not deserve it.

o: The church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments.
A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.
The Greek form (Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6) of the Hebrew Hallelujah = Praise ye Jehovah, which begins or ends several of the psalms (106, 111, 112, 113, etc.).
ch.s: This chapter covers: The church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments (vv. 1–10); A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies (vv. 11–21). People named: Alleluia.
ch.mh: Praising God for what we have, is praying for what is yet further to be done for us.
q: Read verses 1–10 (The church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 11–21 (A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies), what do you learn about war and conflict?
Verse 1 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Revelation 7:10–12. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Alleluia’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of leadership and kingship in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: God has given a rule to walk by, in his word; neither the example of the most, nor of the chief, must influence us contrary thereto: if we do as the most do, we must go where the most go, even into the burning lake.
ch.a: Write down three things this chapter shows about God and thank Him for each.

o: Satan is bound for a thousand years.
The first resurrection; those are blessed that have part therein.
Satan loosed, Gog and Magog.
The last and general resurrection.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.

He is also called "the dragon," "the old serpent" (Rev. 12:9; 20:2); "the prince of this world" (John 12:31; 14:30); "the prince of the power of the air" (Eph. 2:2); "the god of this world" (2 Cor. 4:4); "the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Eph. 2:2). The distinct personality of Satan and his activity among men are thus obviously recognized.

The name of the leader of the hostile party described in Ezek. 38, 39, as coming from the "north country" and assailing the people of Israel to their own destruction. This prophecy has been regarded as fulfilled in the conflicts of the Maccabees with Antiochus, the invasion and overthrow of the Chaldeans, and the temporary successes and destined overthrow of the Turks.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Satan is bound for a thousand years (vv. 1–3); The first resurrection; those are blessed that have part therein (vv. 4–6); Satan loosed, Gog and Magog (vv. 7–10); The last and general resurrection (vv. 11–15). People named: Satan, Gog, Magog.
ch.mh: Here is a vision, showing by a figure the restraints laid on Satan himself.
q: Read verses 1–3 (Satan is bound for a thousand years). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 4–6 (The first resurrection; those are blessed that have part therein), what do you learn about god's sovereignty?
Verse 12 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 2 Corinthians 5:10. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Satan’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of eternal life and resurrection in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We may easily perceive what a variety of dreadful pains, diseases, and other calamities would cease, if all men were true and consistent Christians.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.

o: A new heaven, and new earth: the new Jerusalem where God dwells, and banishes all sorrow from his people.
Its heavenly origin, glory, and secure defence.
Its perfect happiness, as enlightened with the presence of God and the Lamb, and in the free access of multitudes, made holy.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.

THE APOSTLE, brother of James the "Greater" (Matt. 4:21; 10:2; Mark 1:19; 3:17; 10:35). He was one, probably the younger, of the sons of Zebedee (Matt. 4:21) and Salome (Matt. 27:56; comp. Mark 15:40), and was born at Bethsaida.
(Rev. 1:8), the last letter in the Greek alphabet. (See A.)
ch.s: This chapter covers: A new heaven, and new earth: the new Jerusalem where God dwells, and banishes all sorrow from his people (vv. 1–8); Its heavenly origin, glory, and secure defence (vv. 9–21); Its perfect happiness, as enlightened with the presence of God and the Lamb, and in the free access of multitudes, made holy (vv. 22–27). People named: John, Omega, On. Places: Jerusalem.
ch.mh: The new heaven and the new earth will not be separate from each other; the earth of the saints, their glorified, bodies, will be heavenly.
q: Read verses 1–8 (A new heaven, and new earth: the new Jerusalem where God dwells, and banishes all sorrow from his people). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–21 (Its heavenly origin, glory, and secure defence), what do you learn about worship and praise?
Verse 3 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Ezekiel 37:27. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does John’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of holiness in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: As nothing unclean can enter heaven, let us be stirred up by these glimpses of heavenly things, to use all diligence, and to perfect holiness in the fear of God.
ch.a: Write down three things this chapter shows about God and thank Him for each.

o: A description of the heavenly state, under the figures of the water and the tree of life, and of the throne of God and the Lamb.
The truth and certain fulfilling of all the prophetic visions, The Holy Spirit, and the bride, the church, invite, and say, Come.
The closing blessing.
bg: The Apocalypse, the closing book and the only prophetical book of the New Testament canon. The author of this book was undoubtedly John the apostle.

THE APOSTLE, brother of James the "Greater" (Matt. 4:21; 10:2; Mark 1:19; 3:17; 10:35). He was one, probably the younger, of the sons of Zebedee (Matt. 4:21) and Salome (Matt. 27:56; comp. Mark 15:40), and was born at Bethsaida.
(Rev. 1:8), the last letter in the Greek alphabet. (See A.)
ch.s: This chapter covers: A description of the heavenly state, under the figures of the water and the tree of life, and of the throne of God and the Lamb (vv. 1–5); The truth and certain fulfilling of all the prophetic visions, The Holy Spirit, and the bride, the church, invite, and say, Come (vv. 6–19); The closing blessing (vv. 20,21). People named: John, Omega, David.
ch.mh: All streams of earthly comfort are muddy; but these are clear, and refreshing.
q: Read verses 1–5 (A description of the heavenly state, under the figures of the water and the tree of life, and of the throne of God and the Lamb). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 6–19 (The truth and certain fulfilling of all the prophetic visions, The Holy Spirit, and the bride, the church, invite, and say, Come), what do you learn about prophecy and fulfillment?
Verse 1 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Revelation 7:17. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does John’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of holiness in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Revelation?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us earnestly thirst after greater measures of the gracious influences of the blessed Jesus in our souls, and his gracious presence with us, till glory has made perfect his grace toward us.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.
